name: Figstack
tagline: AI helper that explains, documents and translates code.
best_for: Developers reading unfamiliar or legacy code
description:
Figstack is an AI coding assistant aimed at the reading side of programming. Paste a snippet and it describes in plain language what the code does, which helps when you inherit a project with thin documentation or a function written in a language you rarely touch.

Beyond explanations it can draft function documentation and translate code from one programming language to another. It runs in the browser as a web app and through an extension, and the listing says it connects with code editors too. Junior developers can use it to check their understanding, while seniors may lean on it for quick documentation drafts. As with any generated explanation, treat it as a starting point and verify against the real behaviour. Check the official site for current plans and limits.
use_steps: Open the Figstack web app or install the extension.
Paste the code you want to understand.
Pick explain, document or translate for the task at hand.
Read the output, correct anything wrong and copy it into your project.
pros: Handles documentation and translation in one place
cons: Generated explanations can be wrong or shallow
Limits and features depend on the plan
use_cases: Porting a snippet to another language
pricing_details: A free tier exists with paid plans for advanced features and teams, per the listing. Plans change, so check the official site.

faq.a: It explains code in plain language, drafts function documentation and translates code between programming languages.

name: Google Gemini
tagline: Google's multimodal AI assistant for chat, coding and creation.

Gemini is Google's AI assistant, built on its Gemini family of models. You talk to it in text or voice, upload images, and ask for anything from explanations and drafts to debugging help. It is multimodal, so one conversation can mix text, code, pictures, audio and video.


What sets it apart for many people is the tie to Google's ecosystem: the listing mentions links to Gmail, Docs, Android and Workspace, and availability inside developer tools such as AI Studio and Vertex AI. Developers can use it for agent-style coding and quick interface prototypes, and heavier reasoning modes exist for complex problems. A free tier covers everyday use, and higher limits come with paid Google plans. Always verify code and facts it produces, and check the official site for current plans and model names.

Type or speak a task, or upload an image or file.

name: Tempo
tagline: Visual React editor with AI agents that write the code.
best_for: Designers, product managers and engineers building React interfaces
description:
Tempo is a visual IDE for React that pairs a drag-and-drop canvas with AI agents. You edit layout, props and styles visually while the tool updates the underlying code, or you describe a change in words and let an agent make it.


It can import an existing repository, then commit to branches and open pull requests through Git, which makes it more than a throwaway prototyper. The listing also mentions turning requirement documents and wireframes into components, a store of connectors for things like payments and auth, live preview with automatic error fixes, and a local mode for privacy. That mix suits mixed teams where designers and developers touch the same codebase. Generated code still needs review before it ships. Check the official site for current plans and prompt limits.

name: Thunkable
tagline: No-code builder for native iOS and Android apps.
best_for: Students, educators and founders prototyping mobile apps without coding
description:
Thunkable is a browser-based no-code platform for making native mobile apps. You drag components onto a screen to design the interface, then snap together logic blocks to define what happens when someone taps, scrolls or submits something.


One project can be published as both an iOS and an Android app. You can test on a real phone through the companion Thunkable Live app while you build, and connect services such as Google Sheets, Airtable, Firebase and OpenAI for data and AI features. The block approach is gentle for beginners and classrooms, though complex apps can get unwieldy compared with hand-written code. The free tier covers building and testing, while private projects and store publishing need a paid plan. Check the official site for current limits.
use_steps: Create a project and drag components onto the first screen.
Add logic blocks to control behaviour.
Test live on your phone with the companion app.
Connect data sources, then publish to the app stores on a paid plan.
pros: One project for iOS and Android
Live testing on a real device
cons: Large apps can get hard to manage in blocks
Publishing and private projects need a paid plan
features: Integrations such as Airtable and Firebase
pricing_details: A free tier lets you build and test; paid plans cover private projects, storage and store publishing. Plans change, so check the official site.

faq.q: Do I need to code to use Thunkable?
faq.a: No. Interfaces are dragged together and behaviour is built from logic blocks.

faq.a: Yes, but publishing to Apple and Google stores needs a paid plan, per the listing.

name: ViewComfy
tagline: Turn ComfyUI workflows into web apps and serverless APIs.

description:
ViewComfy takes workflows built in ComfyUI and wraps them as simple web apps or serverless APIs. The people using the result see a tidy interface instead of a node graph, while the original workflow stays private.


It has an open-source builder you can self-host, plus a managed cloud for teams that want hosting and support. The listing describes serverless GPUs that scale to zero when idle, support for custom nodes and models, logs and streaming on the API side, and Python and TypeScript integration. You can also share apps by email, control access and track usage. It fits studios that generate images or video through ComfyUI and want clients or colleagues to run them without learning the tool. You still need a working ComfyUI workflow first. Check the official site for current cloud plans.

name: Freu AI
tagline: macOS agent that records a workflow once and replays it locally.
best_for: Mac users repeating the same multi-app tasks
description:
Freu AI is a desktop automation agent for macOS. You show it a workflow once using natural-language prompts, and it compiles that into a fixed command sequence rather than asking a model to improvise every time.


Because it anchors steps to meaningful interface elements instead of screen coordinates, the compiled workflow is meant to survive window resizing and small app updates. Runs happen locally on your Mac without per-run AI calls, which is its main pitch for repetitive jobs like pulling PDF data into a spreadsheet or syncing information between native apps. The listing also mentions an open-source browser automation CLI and a planned on-device vision engine that is not yet available. It is a young product, so test on a harmless task first.
